passage: In the hostel dining hall, someone started a rhyme about Hansa's two long plaits, and the whole table cracked up. Santosh laughed with them, though his laugh came out too loud. Then he saw Hansa's tray trembling and her eyes fixed on her plate, and the laugh stuck in his throat. He knew why he had joined in: he could not bear being the one left alone at the end of the bench. The next evening, when the same boy began the rhyme again, Santosh looked at his rice and did not laugh. Then he picked up his tray and sat down across from Hansa. "Hi," he said. It was small, and a little scary, but the rhyme fizzled out.

qa.q: Where did the rhyme about Hansa's plaits take place?
qa.a: It took place in the hostel dining hall.

qa.q: Why did Santosh laugh at the rhyme about Hansa?
qa.a: He did not want to be left out or end up alone at the end of the bench, so he went along with everyone else.

qa.q: What small refusals did Santosh make the next evening, and what effect did they have?
qa.a: He did not laugh and he moved to sit across from Hansa, and the rhyme fizzled out without an audience.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Santosh sat across from her?
qa.a: She may have felt some relief at a bit of kindness after the laughter, though the passage does not say how she reacted.

grounding: A child laughs because everyone does, sees the target's hurt, and next time refuses and moves to sit with her.

passage:
Monday. In the lunch line, Tanvir said Sharmila's hair looked like a broom. Everyone laughed. Mahima laughed too, even though she didn't think it was funny. She just didn't want to be the only one not laughing.
Wednesday. Tanvir tried another joke about Sharmila. The laughter was louder this time. Mahima laughed again, but her face felt stiff.
That evening she thought about it. Every time she laughed, Tanvir got louder.
Friday. Tanvir started again. Mahima didn't laugh. She picked up her tray and went to sit next to Sharmila. "Can I sit here?" Sharmila nodded. Two other girls followed Mahima.

qa.q: What did Tanvir say Sharmila's hair looked like?
Why did Mahima laugh even though she didn't think it was funny?
qa.a: She was afraid of being left out, and didn't want to be the only one not laughing.

qa.q: What small refusal did Mahima make on Friday?
qa.a: She didn't laugh and went to sit next to Sharmila, and two other girls followed her.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see it when three girls go to sit with Sharmila?
qa.a: Tanvir may feel his audience slipping away, since the laughter that made him stronger has stopped.

grounding: A girl laughs at a classmate because everyone else does, sees it makes the teaser stronger, then refuses to laugh and sits with the target.

passage:
"Bhupen, your Ujjwal Dada once laughed at something he shouldn't have. I was twelve. A boy in our class, Moti, stammered when he read aloud. The class leader started copying him, and everyone laughed, so I laughed too. I didn't want to be the odd one out.
For weeks it went on, and it got worse. The leader got bolder every time we laughed.
One day, Moti's reading made the leader start again. I didn't laugh. I just looked out of the window. Then my friend stopped laughing too. Then another boy.
It wasn't a big speech. We just stopped. And the leader stopped too, because nobody was laughing."

qa.q: What was Moti's difficulty when reading aloud?
Why did young Ujjwal laugh at Moti?
qa.a: He felt anxious about being the odd one out, so he went along with the class even though it wasn't right.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the leader stop?
qa.a: When young Ujjwal stopped laughing and looked away, and others followed, so the leader had no audience.

qa.q: How might Moti have felt when the laughing stopped?
qa.a: Moti may have felt relief and some safety, as reading aloud no longer brought mockery.

grounding: A grandfather recalls laughing along to fit in, seeing it make the teaser bolder, then refusing to laugh, which others copied until the teasing stopped.
